claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
Untreated W–Cu composites undergo phase separation and interfacial void formation under the stated service conditions.
Magnetron sputtering can be used to pre-coat the tungsten particles or ligaments with a Ti–Ni interfacial layer.
A suitably tailored high-entropy alloy can alternatively be used as the sputtered coating on tungsten.
The deposited coating will be conformal and nanoscale on both W particles and interconnected W ligaments.
The coating forms a graded interface between tungsten and copper.
The interfacial coating lowers interfacial energy.
The coating chemically stabilizes the W–Cu contact region.
The coating acts as a diffusive barrier that reduces the effects of intrinsic W–Cu immiscibility.
The coating improves chemical compatibility and interfacial bonding.
Improved interfacial compatibility suppresses phase separation in W–Cu.
The coating prevents nucleation of interfacial voids under thermal and irradiation stresses.
Suppressing phase separation and void formation preserves continuous heat-conduction pathways.
The coated W–Cu composite will have fewer interfacial voids and less phase separation than the untreated composite.
The coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite under operational conditions.
High temperature, high heat flux, and intense energetic-neutron flux are relevant service conditions for W plasma-facing materials coupled to Cu-based heat sinks.
Performance under extremely rapid thermal cycling or non-standard irradiation spectra is uncertain.
The optimal coating composition, thickness, uniformity, and manufacturing scalability remain uncertain.
Failure to obtain statistically significant reductions in both interfacial defects and phase separation together with improved thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.
